newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African vigilantes ally with political party.
newsitem.headline: S.African vigilantes ally with political party.

text.p: A South African Moslem-based vigilante group and the radical black Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) said on Thursday they had formed an anti-crime alliance.

"We are prepared to work with any organisation or grouping of people who we share a common concern with...and insofar as PAGAD (People Against Gangsterism and Drugs) pursues those goals, the PAC will work with them," PAC spokesman and parliamentarian Khaliphile Sizani told a news conference.
PAGAD sprang to prominence in August when members publicly shot and torched to death a well-known drug lord.
Since then the organisation has staged violent protests at Cape Town's international airport and at its premier tourist spot, a waterfront shopping and entertainment centre.
PAGAD commander Aslam Toefy, who faces criminal charges arising from the airport demonstration, told the news conference after talks with PAC representatives:
"What came out clearly of this meeting is that, yes, we are going to fight this thing collectively and the issue at stake here is drugs and all forms of gangsterism."

The PAC broke away from Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) in 1959. In recent years it has fallen on hard times, running out of cash and gaining only five seats in parliament in the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
Since its banning in 1960 the PAC has had strong links with Qibla, a radical Moslem movement calling for the establishment of an Islamic state in South Africa by the year 2000.
PAGAD has over the past weeks placed newspaper advertisements with a political tone, criticising Mandela's government for legalising abortion and failing to crack down on crime.
